questions.question: Consider the star network shown in Figure. The resistance between terminals A and B with C open is \(6\ \Omega\), between terminals B and C with A open is \(11\ \Omega\), and between terminals C and A with B open is \(9\ \Omega\). Then
questions.explanation: Given, \[R_{AB}=6\Omega, \quad \text{with terminal C open.}\] Hence, \[R_A+R_B=6 \tag{1}\] Similarly, \[R_{BC}=11\Omega, \quad \text{with terminal A open.}\] \[R_B+R_C=11 \tag{2}\] Also, \[R_{CA}=9\Omega, \quad \text{with terminal B open.}\] \[R_C+R_A=9 \tag{3}\] Adding (1), (2) and (3), \[2(R_A+R_B+R_C) = 6+11+9\] \[2(R_A+R_B+R_C) = 26\] \[R_A+R_B+R_C = 13 \tag{4}\] From (4) and (2), \[R_A = 13-11 = 2\Omega\] From (1) and (2), \[R_B = 6-2 = 4\Omega, \qquad R_C = 11-4 = 7\Omega\] Hence, \[\boxed{\textbf{B. }R_A=2\Omega,\;R_B=4\Omega,\;R_C=7\Omega}\]

questions.subject: network-theory
questions.question: A unit step voltage is applied at \(t = 0\) to a series RL circuit with zero initial conditions.
options: It is possible for the current to be oscillatory.
The voltage across the resistor at \(t = 0^{+}\) is zero.
The energy stored in the inductor in the steady state is zero.
The resistor current eventually falls to zero.
questions.explanation: For a series \(RL\) circuit excited by a unit-step voltage and having zero initial conditions, \[i(0^-)=0\] Since the current through an inductor cannot change instantaneously, \[i(0^+)=i(0^-)=0\] The steady-state current is \[i(\infty)=\frac{V}{R}\] and the current response is \[i(t)=i(\infty)+\big[i(0^+)-i(\infty)\big]e^{-t/\tau}\] where \[\tau=\frac{L}{R}\] Substituting \(i(0^+)=0\), \[i(t)=\frac{V}{R}\left(1-e^{-Rt/L}\right)\] Option A: It is possible for the current to be oscillatory. Incorrect. A series \(RL\) circuit contains only one energy-storage element and is therefore a first-order circuit. Its response is exponential and cannot be oscillatory. Option B: The voltage across the resistor at \(t=0^+\) is zero. Correct. Since \[i(0^+)=0\] the resistor voltage is \[v_R(0^+)=i(0^+)R=0\] Option C: The energy stored in the inductor in steady state is zero. Incorrect. At steady state, \[i(\infty)=\frac{V}{R}\neq 0\] Hence, the energy stored in the inductor is \[W_L=\frac{1}{2}Li^2(\infty) =\frac{1}{2}L\left(\frac{V}{R}\right)^2\] which is non-zero. Option D: The resistor current eventually falls to zero. Incorrect. Since the resistor and inductor are in series, both carry the same current. As \(t\to\infty\), \[i(\infty)=\frac{V}{R}\] which is a non-zero constant. Therefore, the resistor current does not fall to zero. Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{B. }\text{The voltage across the resistor at \(t = 0^{+}\) is zero.}}\]

questions.question: Two incandescent light bulbs of \(40\text{ W}\) and \(60\text{ W}\) rating are connected in series across the mains. Then
questions.explanation: For a bulb rated at voltage \(V\) and power \(P\), \[R=\frac{V^2}{P}\] Hence, \[R_{40}=\frac{V^2}{40}, \qquad R_{60}=\frac{V^2}{60}\] Therefore, \[R_{40}>R_{60}\] Since the bulbs are connected in series, the same current flows through both bulbs. Power dissipated in each bulb is \[P=I^2R\] Thus, \[P_{40}=I^2R_{40}, \qquad P_{60}=I^2R_{60}\] Since \[R_{40}>R_{60} \ \Rightarrow \ P_{40}>P_{60}\] Hence the \(40\,\text{W}\) bulb dissipates more power and glows brighter. Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{D. }\text{the 40 W bulb glows brighter}}\]

questions.question: In a series RLC circuit at resonance, the magnitude of the voltage developed across the capacitor
options: can never be greater than the input voltage
can be greater than the input voltage, however it is \(90^{\circ}\) out of phase with the input voltage
can be greater than the input voltage, and is in phase with the input voltage
questions.explanation: In a series RLC circuit we know that at resonance,'\[|VL|=|V_C|=Q|V_R|\] where Q is the quality factor which can also be greater than 1. Also at resonance, \[V_R=V_{in}\] Hence we can conclude that it is possible for \(|V_C|\) to be greater than the input voltage. In a series RLC circuit current flowing through all 3 network elements are equal, say I. The current I is equal to \(V_{in}/R\) at resonance and is in phase with input voltage. Thus we can write \[V_C=I\times -jX_C\] Since \(V_C\) lags I by \(90^{\circ}\), we can say that it is \(90^{\circ}\) out of phase with the input voltage as well. \[\boxed{(c)\text{can be greater than the input voltage, however it is $90^{\circ}$ out of phase with the input voltage}}\]

questions.subject: network-theory
questions.question: A 240 V single-phase ac source is connected to a load with an impedance of \(10\angle60^{\circ}\Omega\). A capacitor is connected in parallel with the load. If the capacitor supplied 1250 VAR, the real power supplied by the source is
questions.explanation: Real power will only be absorbed by the load resistance and not by pure reactive components such as an ideal capacitor. First, we determine the load current \(I_L\) flowing through the branch impedance by applying Ohm's law: \[I_L = \frac{V}{Z_L}\] Given parameters from the circuit setup: System voltage, \(V = 240 \angle 0^\circ\,\text{V}\) Load branch impedance, \(Z_L = 10 \angle 60^\circ\,\Omega\) Substituting these values into the current expression: \[I_L = \frac{240 \angle 0^\circ}{10 \angle 60^\circ} = 24 \angle -60^\circ\,\text{A}\] The formula for active real power \(P\) delivered to a circuit branch is given by: \[P = V_L I_L \cos\phi_L\] Where \(V_L\) represents the voltage magnitude across the load branch, \(I_L\) represents the current magnitude, and \(\phi_L\) represents the power factor phase angle between the voltage and current. Extracting the parameters for power evaluation: Voltage magnitude, \(V_L = 240\,\text{V}\) Current magnitude, \(I_L = 24\,\text{A}\) Phase angle, \(\phi_L = 60^\circ\) Substituting these terms to calculate the total absorbed real power: \[P = 240 \times 24 \times \cos(60^\circ)\] \[P = 5760 \times 0.5 = 2880\,\text{W}\] \[\boxed{(b)2880W}\]

questions.subject: network-theory
questions.question: A passive 2-port network is in a steady-state. Compared to its input, the steady state output can never offer
questions.explanation: A network is classified as passive if it contains no internal independent energy sources or amplification mechanisms (such as operational amplifiers or biased transistors). It can only consist of passive circuit elements: resistors (\(R\)), inductors (\(L\)), and capacitors (\(C\)). Let us analyze each of the parameters given in the options: Option A: A passive network can amplify voltage amplitudes under specific steady-state alternating current (\(\text{AC}\)) conditions. For example, a resonant series \(RLC\) tank circuit or a step-up transformer can provide a steady-state output voltage magnitude that is significantly higher than the input voltage magnitude (\(V_{out} > V_{in}\)). Option B: The output impedance or equivalent impedance seen looking into a port can easily be altered, transformed, or made lower than the source impedance by utilizing matching networks or passive transformations. Option C: By the law of conservation of energy (specifically Tellegen's Theorem applied to passive systems), the total real power consumed by the passive components must be greater than or equal to zero (\(P_{\text{consumed}} \ge 0\)). Therefore, the steady-state real power delivered at the output port (\(P_{out}\)) can never exceed the real power injected into the input port (\(P_{in}\)): \[P_{out} \le P_{in}\] Hence, a passive two-port network can never offer greater power at its output compared to its input. Option D: Voltage regulation is a measure of a network's ability to maintain a constant output voltage under varying load conditions. Passive networks can alter regulation attributes depending on their structural impedances. Thus, the strict physical limitation imposed by passivity ensures that the network can never amplify power. \[\boxed{(c)\textit{Greater power}}\]

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: Consider the voltage waveform \(v\), shown in figure. Find
options: The amplitude of the fundamental component of \(v\), and
The RMS value of the ac part of \(v\).
questions.explanation:
(A) DC Component
\[V_{\text{DC}} =\frac{3(1)+2(-1)}{5} =0.2\,\text{V}.\] \[\boxed{V_{\text{DC}}=0.2\,\text{V}}\] (B) The amplitude of the fundamental component of \(v\)
To find the amplitude of the fundamental component, we use the trigonometric Fourier series. The amplitude \(C_1\) of the fundamental frequency is given by \(C_1 = \sqrt{a_1^2 + b_1^2}\), where \(a_1\) and \(b_1\) are the first Fourier coefficients. Step 1: Calculate \(a_1\)
\[\begin{aligned} a_1 &= \frac{2}{T} \int_{0}^{T} v(t) \cos(\omega_0 t) \,dt \\ a_1 &= \frac{2}{5} \left[ \int_{0}^{3} (1)\cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{5}t\right) \,dt + \int_{3}^{5} (-1)\cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{5}t\right) \,dt \right] \\ a_1 &= \frac{2}{5} \left[ \frac{5}{2\pi} \sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{5}t\right) \Bigg|_{0}^{3} - \frac{5}{2\pi} \sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{5}t\right) \Bigg|_{3}^{5} \right] \\ a_1 &= \frac{1}{\pi} \left[ \left(\sin\left(\frac{6\pi}{5}\right) - 0\right) - \left(\sin(2\pi) - \sin\left(\frac{6\pi}{5}\right)\right) \right] \end{aligned}\] Since \(\sin(2\pi) = 0\): \[\begin{aligned} a_1 &= \frac{1}{\pi} \left[ 2\sin\left(\frac{6\pi}{5}\right) \right] = \frac{2}{\pi} \sin\left(\frac{6\pi}{5}\right) \end{aligned}\] Step 2: Calculate \(b_1\)
\[\begin{aligned} b_1 &= \frac{2}{T} \int_{0}^{T} v(t) \sin(\omega_0 t) \,dt \\ b_1 &= \frac{2}{5} \left[ \int_{0}^{3} (1)\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{5}t\right) \,dt - \int_{3}^{5} \sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{5}t\right) \,dt \right] \\ b_1 &= \frac{2}{5} \left[ -\frac{5}{2\pi} \cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{5}t\right) \Bigg|_{0}^{3} + \frac{5}{2\pi} \cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{5}t\right) \Bigg|_{3}^{5} \right] \\ b_1 &= \frac{1}{\pi} \left[ \left(-\cos\left(\frac{6\pi}{5}\right) + \cos(0)\right) + \left(\cos(2\pi) - \cos\left(\frac{6\pi}{5}\right)\right) \right] \end{aligned}\] Since \(\cos(0) = 1\) and \(\cos(2\pi) = 1\): \[\begin{aligned} b_1 &= \frac{1}{\pi} \left[ 2 - 2\cos\left(\frac{6\pi}{5}\right) \right] = \frac{2}{\pi} \left[ 1 - \cos\left(\frac{6\pi}{5}\right) \right] \end{aligned}\] Step 3: Calculate Amplitude \(C_1\)
\[\begin{aligned} C_1 &= \sqrt{a_1^2 + b_1^2} \\ C_1 &= \sqrt{ \left(\frac{2}{\pi} \sin\left(\frac{6\pi}{5}\right)\right)^2 + \left(\frac{2}{\pi} \left(1 - \cos\left(\frac{6\pi}{5}\right)\right)\right)^2 } \\ C_1 &= \frac{2}{\pi} \sqrt{ \sin^2\left(\frac{6\pi}{5}\right) + 1 - 2\cos\left(\frac{6\pi}{5}\right) + \cos^2\left(\frac{6\pi}{5}\right) } \end{aligned}\] Using the identity \(\sin^2(\theta) + \cos^2(\theta) = 1\): \[\begin{aligned} C_1 &= \frac{2}{\pi} \sqrt{ 2 - 2\cos\left(\frac{6\pi}{5}\right) } = \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\pi} \sqrt{ 1 - \cos\left(\frac{6\pi}{5}\right) } \end{aligned}\] Using the half-angle formula \(1 - \cos(\theta) = 2\sin^2\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\): \[\begin{aligned} C_1 &= \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\pi} \sqrt{ 2\sin^2\left(\frac{3\pi}{5}\right) } = \frac{4}{\pi} \sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{5}\right) \end{aligned}\] \[\boxed{\text{The amplitude of the fundamental component is $\frac{4}{\pi} \sin\left(\frac{3\pi}{5}\right)\text{ V}$ (approximately 1.21 V)}}\] (C) The RMS value of the ac part of \(v\)
The total RMS value of a waveform squared is equal to the sum of the DC component squared and the AC RMS component squared: \[\begin{aligned} V_{rms}^2 &= V_{dc}^2 + V_{ac,rms}^2 \end{aligned}\] Step 1: Find the total RMS value (\(V_{rms}\))
Since the waveform simply alternates between \(1\text{ V}\) and \(-1\text{ V}\), the squared waveform \(v^2(t)\) is constantly \(1\text{ V}^2\) for the entire period. \[\begin{aligned} V_{rms} &= \sqrt{\frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^{T} v^2(t) \,dt} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{5} \int_{0}^{5} (1)^2 \,dt} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{5} [5]} = 1\text{ V} \end{aligned}\] Step 2: Solve for \(V_{ac,rms}\)
Using the values we found earlier (\(V_{rms} = 1\text{ V}\) and \(V_{dc} = 0.2\text{ V}\)): \[\begin{aligned} (1)^2 &= (0.2)^2 + V_{ac,rms}^2 \\ 1 &= 0.04 + V_{ac,rms}^2 \\ V_{ac,rms}^2 &= 0.96 \\ V_{ac,rms} &= \sqrt{0.96} = \sqrt{\frac{96}{100}} = \frac{4\sqrt{6}}{10} = \frac{2\sqrt{6}}{5} \end{aligned}\] \[\boxed{\text{The RMS value of the ac part is $\sqrt{0.96}\text{ V}$ or $\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{5}V$ (approximately 0.98 V)}}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: An op-amp has an open-loop gain of \(10^5\) and an open-loop upper cutoff frequency of \(10\text{ Hz}\). If this op-amp is connected as an amplifier with a closed gain of \(100\), then the new upper cutoff frequency is
questions.explanation:
The gain-bandwidth product (\(\text{GBW}\)) of an operational amplifier remains constant: \[A_1 \times f_{c1} = A_2 \times f_{c2}\] Given parameters:
  • Open-loop gain, \(A_1 = 10^5\)
  • Open-loop upper cutoff frequency, \(f_{c1} = 10\,\text{Hz}\)
  • Closed-loop gain, \(A_2 = 100\)
Substituting the values: \[10^5 \times 10\,\text{Hz} = 100 \times f_{c2}\] \[f_{c2} = \frac{10^6}{10^2} = 10^4\,\text{Hz} = 10\,\text{kHz}\] Due to negative feedback, the gain decreases while the bandwidth increases proportionally. \[\boxed{(c) \ \ \text{10\text{ kHz}}}\]
Key points
Gain-Bandwidth Product Conservation: For a single-pole op-amp, \(A_{\text{OL}} \cdot f_H = \text{GBW} = \text{constant}\). Introducing negative feedback trades gain for an equal factor increase in bandwidth.

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: For the oscillator circuit shown in figure, the expression for the time period of oscillation can be given by (where \(\tau = RC\))
questions.explanation:
The non-inverting terminal voltage \(V_+\) via potential divider is: \[V_+ = V_{\text{o}} \times \frac{R}{R + R} = \frac{V_{\text{o}}}{2}\] Assuming \(V_{\text{o}} = -V_{\text{sat}}\), then \(V_+ = -\frac{V_{\text{sat}}}{2}\). When \(V_{\text{c}}\) drops below \(-\dfrac{V_{\text{sat}}}{2}\), \(V_{\text{o}}\) switches to \(+V_{\text{sat}}\), giving \(V_+ = +\dfrac{V_{\text{sat}}}{2}\). The capacitor charges towards \(V_{\text{c}}(\infty) = +V_{\text{sat}}\) from \(V_{\text{c}}(0) = -\dfrac{V_{\text{sat}}}{2}\): \[V_{\text{c}}(t) = V_{\text{c}}(\infty) + [V_{\text{c}}(0) - V_{\text{c}}(\infty)]e^{-t/\tau}\] \[V_{\text{c}}(t) = V_{\text{sat}} - \dfrac{3}{2}V_{\text{sat}}e^{-t/\tau}\] The output switches state again when \(V_{\text{c}}(t) = \frac{V_{\text{sat}}}{2}\): \[\frac{V_{\text{sat}}}{2} = V_{\text{sat}} - \frac{3}{2}V_{\text{sat}}e^{-t/\tau}\] \[\frac{3}{2}e^{-t/\tau} = \frac{1}{2} \implies e^{t/\tau} = 3 \implies t = \tau \ln 3\] Since charging and discharging intervals are equal, the total time period \(T\) is: \[T = 2t = 2\tau \ln 3\] \[\boxed{(B) \ \ 2\tau \ln 3}\]
Key points
Astable Multivibrator: For an op-amp relaxation oscillator with feedback factor \(\beta = \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}\), the time period of oscillation is given by \(T = 2\tau \ln\left(\frac{1+\beta}{1-\beta}\right)\). Here, \(\beta = \frac{1}{2}\), giving \(T = 2\tau \ln 3\).

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: An op-amp having a slew rate of \(62.8\text{ V}/\mu\text{sec}\) is connected in a voltage follower configuration. If the maximum amplitude of the input sinusoidal is \(10\text{ Volts}\), then the minimum frequency at which the slew rate limited distortion would set in the output is
questions.explanation:
To avoid distortion, the maximum rate of change of the output voltage must not exceed the slew rate (\(\text{S.R.}\)): \[\text{S.R.} \ge \left( \frac{\text{d}V_{\text{o}}}{\text{d}t} \right)_{\max}\] For a sinusoidal output \(V_{\text{o}}(t) = V_{\text{m}} \sin(\omega t)\): \[\left( \frac{\text{d}V_{\text{o}}}{\text{d}t} \right)_{\max} = V_{\text{m}} \omega = 2\pi f V_{\text{m}}\] Given \(\text{S.R.} = 62.8\text{ V}/\mu\text{s} = 62.8 \times 10^6\text{ V}/\text{s}\) and \(V_{\text{m}} = 10\text{ V}\): \[62.8 \times 10^6 \ge 2\pi f \times 10\] \[f \le \frac{62.8 \times 10^6}{2\pi \times 10} = 10^6\text{ Hz} = 1\text{ MHz}\] Thus, the minimum frequency at which slew-rate limiting distortion sets in is \(1\text{ MHz}\). \[\boxed{\text{(A) $1\text{ MHz}$}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
Always convert the slew rate from \(\text{V}/\mu\text{s}\) to \(\text{V}/\text{s}\) by multiplying by \(10^6\) before calculating frequency in \(\text{Hz}\).

questions.question: For the op-amp circuit shown in figure, determine the output voltage \(V_0\). Assume that the op-amps are ideal.
questions.explanation: Applying superposition for the \(1^{\text{st}}\) Op-Amp: \[V_{\text{o1}} = V_1 \left( \frac{2}{1} + 1 \right) + 1 \times \left( -\frac{2}{1} \right) = 3V_1 - 2\] From the voltage divider network at the non-inverting terminal: \[V_1 = V_{\text{o}} \times \left( \frac{1}{1 + 3} \right) = \frac{V_{\text{o}}}{4}\] Substituting \(V_1\) into \(V_{\text{o1}}\): \[V_{\text{o1}} = 3 \left( \frac{V_{\text{o}}}{4} \right) - 2 = \frac{3}{4}V_{\text{o}} - 2\] Applying superposition for the \(2^{\text{nd}}\) Op-Amp: \[V_{\text{o}} = V_{\text{o1}} \left( -\frac{8}{4} \right) + (-1) \left( 1 + \frac{8}{4} \right) = -2V_{\text{o1}} - 3\] Substituting \(V_{\text{o1}}\) into the equation for \(V_{\text{o}}\): \[V_{\text{o}} = -2 \left( \frac{3}{4}V_{\text{o}} - 2 \right) - 3\] \[V_{\text{o}} = -\frac{3}{2}V_{\text{o}} + 4 - 3 \implies \left( 1 + \frac{3}{2} \right) V_{\text{o}} = 1\] \[\frac{5}{2} V_{\text{o}} = 1 \implies V_{\text{o}} = \frac{2}{5} = 0.4\,\text{V}\] \[\boxed{0.4}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: A simple active filter is shown in Figure. Assume ideal op-amp. Derive the transfer function \(\dfrac{V_0}{V_i}\) of the circuit, and state the type of the filter (i.e., high-pass, low-pass, band-pass, or band-reject). Determine the required values of \(R_1\), \(R_2\) and \(C\) in order for the filter to have a \(3\text{-dB}\) frequency of \(1\text{ kHz}\), a high frequency input resistance of \(100\text{ k}\Omega\), and a high frequency gain magnitude of \(10\).
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
Applying nodal analysis at the inverting terminal: \[\frac{0 - V_{\text{i}}}{R_1 + \frac{1}{sC}} + \frac{0 - V_{\text{o}}}{R_2} = 0\] The transfer function is: \[H(s) = \frac{V_{\text{o}}}{V_{\text{i}}} = \frac{-R_2}{R_1 + \frac{1}{sC}} = \frac{-sCR_2}{1 + sCR_1}\] For \(s = j\omega\), the magnitude response \(|A(\omega)|\) is: \[|A(\omega)| = \left| \frac{V_{\text{o}}}{V_{\text{i}}} \right| = \frac{\omega CR_2}{\sqrt{1 + (\omega CR_1)^2}}\] At \(\omega = 0\), \(A(0) = 0\); and at \(\omega \to \infty\), \(A(\infty) = \frac{R_2}{R_1}\). Thus, the circuit acts as a High-Pass Filter. At high frequencies, \(C\) behaves as a short circuit, so input resistance is \(R_1 = 100\,\text{k}\Omega\). Given \(3\text{-dB}\) cutoff frequency \(f_c = 1\,\text{kHz} = 10^3\,\text{Hz}\): \[f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi R_1 C} = 10^3\] \[C = \frac{1}{2\pi \times 100 \times 10^3 \times 10^3} \approx 1.5915\,\text{nF}\] High frequency gain magnitude \(|A(\infty)| = \left|-\dfrac{R_2}{R_1}\right| = 10\): \[R_2 = 10 R_1 = 10 \times 100\,\text{k}\Omega = 1\,\text{M}\Omega\] \[\boxed{R_1 = 100\,\text{k}\Omega, R_2 = 1\,\text{M}\Omega, C = 1.5915\,\text{nF}}\]
Key points
Active High-Pass Filter: The \(3\text{-dB}\) corner frequency depends on the input RC network \(\omega_c = \frac{1}{R_1 C}\), while the high-frequency passband gain is governed by \(A_v = -\frac{R_2}{R_1}\).

questions.question: The output of a logic gate is ``1'' when all its inputs are at logic ``0''. The gate is either
options: A NAND or an EX-OR gate
A NOR or an EX-OR gate
An AND or an EX-NOR gate
A NOR or an EX-NOR gate
questions.explanation:
Given: Output of a logic gate is ``1'', when all its inputs are at logic ``0''. There are only three gates which produce output~1 when all inputs are~0: NOR, NAND, and EX-NOR. Among the given options, only NOR and EX-NOR appear together. NOR gate:
\[Y_0 = \overline{X+Y}, \qquad Y_0 = 1 \text{ when } X = Y = 0\] EX-NOR gate:
\[Y_0 = XY + \bar{X}\bar{Y}, \qquad Y_0 = 1 \text{ when } X = Y = 0\] EX-OR gate gives \(Y_0 = 0\) when \(X = Y = 0\), so it does not qualify. Hence, the correct option is (D). (D) A NOR or an EX-NOR gate

questions.question: The circuit shown in the figure is a MOD-\(N\) ring counter. Value of \(N\) is (assume initial state of the counter is 1110 i.e. \(Q_3\,Q_2\,Q_1\,Q_0 = 1110\))
questions.explanation:
Given: MOD-\(N\) counter circuit with logic gates. From figure, \[A = \overline{Q_3 + Q_2 + Q_1}\] \[D_3 = A = \overline{Q_3 + Q_2 + Q_1}\] \[D_2 = Q_3\] \[D_1 = Q_2 \qquad \text{and} \qquad D_0 = Q_1\] The truth table for the given circuit is shown below, State Trajectory and Modulus Analysis:
Tracing the sequence from the table starting with the initial configuration \(Q_3Q_2Q_1Q_0 = 1110\):
  • The circuit transitions through a series of initial transient states: \(1110 \rightarrow 0111 \rightarrow 0011 \rightarrow 0001\).
  • Once the circuit reaches the state \(0001\), it enters a closed, self-sustaining loop.
The explicitly tracked repeating cycle obtained from the state table is: \[0001 \rightarrow 1000 \rightarrow 0100 \rightarrow 0010 \rightarrow 0001 \rightarrow \dots\] Since this repeating cycle contains exactly four distinct states, the stable count sequence length is 4. The initial states \(1110\), \(0111\), and \(0011\) are transient states that occur only once during power-up and do not factor into the periodic counting behavior. Therefore, it is a MOD-4 counter. Hence, the correct option is (A). (A) 4
Key points
  • The modulus (MOD value) of a sequential counter is determined exclusively by the number of unique states contained within its recurring/periodic loop.
  • Transient states are states that lead into the main cycle but are never revisited once the stable loop is entered.

Statement for Linked Questions (Q1.07.1 and Q1.07.2):
An inductor designed with \(400\) turns coil wound on an iron core of \(16\,\text{cm}^2\) cross sectional area and with a cut of an air gap length of \(1\,\text{mm}\). The coil is connected to a \(230\,\text{V}\), \(50\,\text{Hz}\) ac supply. Neglect coil resistance, core loss, iron reluctance and leakage inductance. \((\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\,\text{H/m})\)

Determine the resonance frequency and the Q-factor of the circuit shown in figure. Data: \(R = 10\,\Omega\), \(C = 3\,\mu\text{F}\), \(L_1 = 40\,\text{mH}\), \(L_2 = 10\,\text{mH}\) and \(M = 10\,\text{mH}\). [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
Let \(i_1\) be the current flowing clockwise in the primary loop and \(i_2\) be the current flowing clockwise in the short-circuited secondary loop. Both currents enter the dotted terminals of their respective inductors. Applying Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) to the secondary loop: \[j\omega L_2 i_2 + j\omega M i_1 = 0\] Expressing \(i_2\) in terms of \(i_1\): \[i_2 = -\frac{M}{L_2} i_1\] Applying KVL to the primary loop: \[V = i_1 R + \frac{i_1}{j\omega C} + j\omega L_1 i_1 + j\omega M i_2\] Substituting \(i_2\) into the primary loop equation: \[V = i_1 \left( R + \frac{1}{j\omega C} + j\omega L_1 - j\omega \frac{M^2}{L_2} \right)\] \[V = i_1 \left( R + j\left( \omega \left( L_1 - \frac{M^2}{L_2} \right) - \frac{1}{\omega C} \right) \right)\] Thus, the net equivalent inductance \(L_{eq}\) of the coupled circuit is: \[L_{eq} = L_1 - \frac{M^2}{L_2}\] Given data: \(L_1 = 40\,\text{mH}\), \(L_2 = 10\,\text{mH}\), and \(M = 10\,\text{mH}\). \[L_{eq} = 40\,\text{mH} - \frac{(10\,\text{mH})^2}{10\,\text{mH}} = 30\,\text{mH} = 30 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{H}\] At resonance, the imaginary part of the total impedance is zero (\(\omega_r L_{eq} = \frac{1}{\omega_r C}\)): \[\omega_r = \frac{1}{\sqrt{L_{eq} C}}\] Given \(C = 3\,\mu\text{F} = 3 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{F}\): \[\omega_r = \frac{1}{\sqrt{30 \times 10^{-3} \times 3 \times 10^{-6}}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{90 \times 10^{-9}}} = \frac{1}{3 \times 10^{-4}} = 3333.33\,\text{rad/s}\] The resonance frequency in Hertz (\(f_r\)) is: \[f_r = \frac{\omega_r}{2\pi} = \frac{3333.33}{2\pi} \approx 530.52\,\text{Hz}\] The Quality factor (\(Q\)-factor) for the series resonant circuit is given by: \[Q = \frac{\omega_r L_{eq}}{R}\] Given \(R = 10\,\Omega\): \[Q = \frac{3333.33 \times 30 \times 10^{-3}}{10} = 10\] \[\boxed{530.52, 10}\]
Key points
  • When a secondary coupled inductor is short-circuited, the reflected impedance modifies the primary self-inductance to an equivalent value: \(L_{eq} = L_1 - \frac{M^2}{L_2}\).
  • The resonance frequency of a series \(R-L-C\) network occurs when inductive reactance equals capacitive reactance: \(\omega_r = \frac{1}{\sqrt{L_{eq}C}}\).
  • The quality factor \(Q\) measures the sharpness of resonance and is defined as \(Q = \frac{\omega_r L_{eq}}{R}\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not ignore the short-circuited secondary loop; the mutual coupling directly reduces the effective inductance of the primary loop.

Statement for Linked Questions (Q1.07.1 and Q1.07.2):
An inductor designed with \(400\) turns coil wound on an iron core of \(16\,\text{cm}^2\) cross sectional area and with a cut of an air gap length of \(1\,\text{mm}\). The coil is connected to a \(230\,\text{V}\), \(50\,\text{Hz}\) ac supply. Neglect coil resistance, core loss, iron reluctance and leakage inductance. \((\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\,\text{H/m})\)

The hysteresis loop of a magnetic material has an area of \(5\text{ cm}^{2}\), with the scales given as \(1\text{ cm} = 2\text{ AT}\) and \(1\text{ cm} = 50\text{ mWb}\). At \(50\text{ Hz}\), the total hysteresis loss is
questions.explanation:
The area of the hysteresis loop represents the energy loss per unit volume per cycle. According to the given scales, the hysteresis energy loss per cycle is calculated as: \[\text{Energy loss per cycle} = \text{Area of the loop} \times (\text{Scale of X-axis} \times \text{Scale of Y-axis})\] Given: Area = \(5\,\text{cm}^2\) Scale of X-axis (Magnetizing force/Current) = \(2\,\text{AT}\) Scale of Y-axis (Flux) = \(50\,\text{mWb}\) \[\text{Energy loss per cycle} = 5 \times (2\,\text{AT} \times 50\,\text{mWb}) = 500\,\text{mJ}\] The total hysteresis power loss (\(P_h\)) at a frequency (\(f\)) of \(50\,\text{Hz}\) is: \[P_h = \text{Energy loss per cycle} \times f\] \[P_h = 500\,\text{mJ} \times 50 = 25000\,\text{mW} = 25\,\text{W}\] \[\boxed{C}\]
Key points
  • Hysteresis loss is the energy dissipated in the form of heat due to the reversal of magnetization of the core.
  • Power loss formula: \(P_h = E_{cycle} \times f\), where \(E_{cycle}\) is the energy loss per cycle (area of the B-H loop) and \(f\) is the frequency.
  • Always account for axis scaling factors when calculating energy from a geometric area.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Forgetting to multiply the area by the frequency to find the power loss (Watts).
  • Incorrectly handling units like milli (\(10^{-3}\)) which can lead to a result of \(25000\) instead of \(25\).

A \(300\,\mathrm{kVA}\) transformer has \(95\%\) efficiency at full load \(0.8\,\mathrm{pf}\) lagging and \(96\%\) efficiency at half load, unity pf. The iron loss \((P_i)\) and copper loss \((P_c)\) in \(\mathrm{kW}\), under full load operation are

A single-phase transformer is to be switched to the supply to have minimum inrush current. The switch should be closed at
questions.explanation: [figure unavailable] Whenever switching takes place in an inductive circuit, transient current is produced and the total current becomes \[i(t)=i_{t}(t)+i_{ss}(t)\] [figure unavailable] where, \[i_{t}(t)\rightarrow \text{Transient component}\] \[i_{ss}(t)\rightarrow \text{Steady-state component}\] Assume an AC input of the form, \[v(t)=V_m\sin(\omega t+\alpha)\] The total current at any instant is \[i(t) = \left[ -\frac{V_m}{\sqrt{R^2+X_L^2}} \sin\left( \alpha-\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\omega L}{R}\right) \right) e^{-Rt/L} \right]\] \[+ \frac{V_m}{\sqrt{R^2+X_L^2}} \sin \left[ \omega t+\alpha - \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{\omega L}{R} \right) \right]\] For transient current to become zero, \[\alpha = \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{\omega L}{R} \right)\] Generally in transformers, \[X\gg R\] Hence, \[\phi = 90^\circ\] Thus voltage-current phase difference is approximately \[90^\circ\] From the waveform, if switching occurs at voltage maximum, current at the switching instant becomes zero and heavy inrush current can be avoided. Switching at voltage minimum \((0^\circ)\) results in maximum current and high inrush current.

A \(300\,\mathrm{kVA}\) transformer has \(95\%\) efficiency at full load \(0.8\,\mathrm{pf}\) lagging and \(96\%\) efficiency at half load, unity pf. The iron loss \((P_i)\) and copper loss \((P_c)\) in \(\mathrm{kW}\), under full load operation are

The core flux of a practical transformer with a resistive load
options: is strictly constant with load changes
increases as the square root of the load
questions.explanation: The core flux of a transformer is determined by the applied voltage-to-frequency ratio: \[\phi \propto \frac{\text{Applied Voltage}}{\text{Applied Frequency}}\] Hence, once the applied voltage and frequency are fixed, the core flux becomes independent of load variations due to the compensation effect in a transformer. During loading, the secondary current produces a flux that opposes the main flux. To maintain the flux constant, the primary draws an additional current component. \[I_{1}=\frac{V_{1}-E_{1}}{Z}\] This extra current compensates for the demagnetizing effect of secondary current. Therefore, the core flux remains approximately constant.

An ideal transformer has a linear \(B/H\) characteristic with a finite slope and a turns ratio of \(1:1\). The primary of the transformer is energized with an ideal current source, producing the signal \(i\) as shown in Fig.Q2.01.4. Sketch the shape (neglecting the scale factor) of the following signals, labeling the time axis clearly: [figure unavailable]
  1. the core flux \(\phi_{oc}\) with the secondary of the transformer open
  2. the open-circuited secondary terminal voltage \(v_2(t)\)
  3. the short-circuited secondary current \(i_2(t)\), and
  4. the core flux \(\phi_{sc}\) with the secondary of the transformer short-circuited.
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
For a linear B-H curve, \[\phi \propto I_{exciting}\] Hence both flux and exciting current have the same waveform. [figure unavailable] Induced emf is given by, \[V_{2}(t)=-N\frac{d\phi}{dt}\] Thus the induced emf waveform is obtained from the derivative of the triangular flux waveform. [figure unavailable] For short-circuit condition, \[R_{2}\rightarrow 0\] Hence the transformer behaves as a purely inductive circuit and short-circuit current lags induced emf approximately by \[90^\circ\] [figure unavailable] Due to transformer action, secondary flux is compensated by additional primary current, therefore net core flux remains unchanged. \[\boxed{*}\]
Key points
  • Core flux in a transformer is determined mainly by applied voltage and frequency.
  • Induced emf is proportional to the rate of change of flux: \[e=-N\frac{d\phi}{dt}\]
  • Under short-circuit condition, additional primary current compensates secondary flux.
  • Therefore transformer core flux waveform remains nearly constant.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume short-circuit condition changes the core flux significantly.
  • Do not confuse flux waveform with induced emf waveform; emf is proportional to the derivative of flux.
  • Current waveform in a highly inductive circuit lags voltage approximately by \(90^\circ\), not in phase.

Statement for Linked Questions Q3.08.1 and Q3.08.2:
A \(240\,\text{V}\), dc shunt motor draws \(15\,\text{A}\) while supplying the rated load at a speed of \(80\,\text{rad/s}\). The armature resistance is \(0.5\,\Omega\) and the field winding resistance is \(80\,\Omega\).

In a dc motor running at \(2000\) rpm, the hysteresis and eddy current losses are \(500\)W and \(200\)W respectively. If the flux remains constant, calculate the speed at which the total iron losses are halved.
questions.explanation:
Given that the flux in the machine is constant, the air-gap flux density \(B\) remains constant. For rotating machines, \[P_{h} \propto B^{1.6}f\] Since \(B\) is constant, \[P_{h} \propto f \propto N\] Also, \[P_{e} \propto B^{2}f^{2}\] Hence, \[P_{e} \propto f^{2} \propto N^{2}\] At \(N=2000\,\text{rpm}\), \[P_{h}=500\,\text{W}\] Therefore, \[P_{h}=k_{h}N\] \[500=k_{h}\times 2000\] \[k_{h}=\frac{500}{2000}=0.25\] Similarly, \[P_{e}=200\,\text{W}\] \[P_{e}=k_{e}N^{2}\] \[200=k_{e}(2000)^{2}\] \[k_{e}=\frac{200}{(2000)^{2}}=5\times10^{-5}\] Initially, total iron loss is \[P_{i}=P_{h}+P_{e}=500+200=700\,\text{W}\] When the iron losses are halved, \[P_{i}=350\,\text{W}\] Let the new speed be \(N'\). \[k_{h}N'+k_{e}N'^{2}=350\] \[0.25N'+5\times10^{-5}N'^{2}=350\] Multiplying throughout by \(20000\), \[5000N'+N'^{2}=700\times10^{4}\] Solving, \[N'=1140\,\text{rpm}\] \[\boxed{1140}\]
Key points
  • Hysteresis loss varies directly with frequency and hence speed when flux density is constant.
  • Eddy current loss varies as the square of frequency and hence as the square of speed.
  • Total iron loss is the sum of hysteresis and eddy current losses.

If the flux at an armature current of \(20\)A is \(0.4\) times of that under rated condition, calculate the speed at this reduced armature current of \(20\)A. [figure unavailable]

At the initial condition, \[E_{b1}=230-(80)(0.25) =210\,\text{V}\] \[E_{b1}=k\phi_1N_1\] Hence, \[k=\frac{210}{\phi_1N_1}\] At the new operating condition, \[E_{b2}=230-(20)(0.25) =225\,\text{V}\] \[E_{b2}=k\phi_2N_2\] Given, \[\phi_2=0.4\phi_1\] Therefore, \[N_2 = \frac{225}{k\phi_2} = \frac{225(\phi_1N_1)} {210(0.4\phi_1)}\] \[N_2 = \frac{225\times 1000} {210\times 0.4} = 2678.57\,\text{rpm}\] \[\boxed{2678.57}\]

It is desirable to eliminate \(5^{\text{th}}\) harmonic voltage from the phase voltage of an alternator. The coils should be short-pitched by an electrical angle of
questions.explanation: To eliminate the \(n^{\text{th}}\) harmonic from the generated emf of an alternator, the coil-span factor for that harmonic must be zero. The pitch factor is \[k_{pn}=\cos\left(\frac{n\alpha}{2}\right)\] where \(\alpha\) is the short-pitch angle. For elimination of the \(5^{\text{th}}\) harmonic, \[k_{p5}=0\] \[\cos\left(\frac{5\alpha}{2}\right)=0\] \[\frac{5\alpha}{2}=90^\circ\] \[\alpha=\frac{180^\circ}{5}\] \[\alpha=36^\circ\] Therefore, the correct option is \[\boxed{\text{B}}\]

Statement for Linked Questions (Q5.05.2 and Q5.05.3):
Statement for Linked Answer Questions 83a & 83b: A \(1000\,\text{kVA}\), \(6.6\,\text{kV}\), \(3\)-phase star connected cylindrical pole synchronous generator has a synchronous reactance of \(20\,\Omega\). Neglect the armature resistance and consider operation at full load and unity power factor.

Fig.P1.8 shows the magnetization curves of an alternator at rated armature current, unity power factor and also at no load. The magnetization curve for rated armature current, \(0.8\) power factor leading is given by [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
[figure unavailable] At short-circuit condition, \[V_t=0\] To produce rated armature current under short-circuit, a non-zero field current is required. Since this field current is the same for leading, lagging and unity power factor loads, all OCC curves must originate from the same point corresponding to the short-circuit field current. Hence, curves A and B are eliminated. Now consider a leading power factor load. For constant armature current and excitation, \[V_t=E_f-jI_aX_s\] For a leading power factor load, \[I_a=I_a\angle 90^\circ\] Therefore, \[V_t=E_f-\left(jI_a\right)\left(jX_s\right)\] \[V_t=E_f+I_aX_s\] Thus, the reactance drop adds to the generated emf, resulting in a higher terminal voltage for the same field current. Hence, the upper curve corresponds to leading power factor operation, while the lower curve corresponds to lagging power factor operation. \[\boxed{\text{C}}\]
Key points
  • At short circuit, \(V_t=0\), but a finite field current is required to produce rated armature current.
  • Leading power factor load produces a voltage rise, whereas lagging power factor load produces a voltage drop.
  • Hence, for the same excitation, the terminal voltage is maximum for leading power factor loading.

A star-connected \(440\,\mathrm{V}\), \(50\,\mathrm{Hz}\) alternators has per phase synchronous reactance of \(10\Omega\). It supplies a balanced capacitive load current of \(20\,\mathrm{A}\), as shown in the per phase equivalent circuit of Fig.2.9. It is desirable to have zero voltage regulation. The load power factor should be [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
For zero voltage regulation, \[\cos(\theta+\phi) = -\frac{|I_a||Z_s|}{2|V_t|}\] Substituting the given values, \[\cos(\theta+\phi) = -\frac{20\times10} {2\times\left(\dfrac{440}{\sqrt{3}}\right)} = -0.3936\] \[\theta+\phi = 113.178^\circ\] Since the synchronous impedance consists only of reactance, \[\theta = 90^\circ\] Therefore, \[\phi = 113.178^\circ-90^\circ = 23.178^\circ\] \[\cos\phi = \cos(23.178^\circ) = 0.92\] Therefore, the correct option is \[\boxed{\text{D}}\]
Key points
  • For zero voltage regulation of a synchronous generator, \[\cos(\theta+\phi) = -\frac{|I_a||Z_s|}{2|V_t|}\]
  • If armature resistance is neglected, the synchronous impedance is purely reactive and \[\theta=90^\circ.\]
  • Zero voltage regulation occurs at a leading power factor load.

questions.explanation: When excitation is OFF for the synchronous motor, the driving motor supplies only the friction and windage losses. \[P_{\text{friction\ \&\ windage}}=800\,\text{W}\] When the armature is short-circuited and rated armature current flows, the input power corresponds to friction and windage losses plus full-load copper losses. \[P_{\text{friction\ \&\ windage}}+P_{\text{cu}}=2500\,\text{W}\] \[P_{\text{cu}}=2500-800=1700\,\text{W}\] With excitation ON and armature open-circuited, the driving motor supplies friction and windage losses and iron losses. \[P_{\text{friction\ \&\ windage}}+P_{\text{iron}}=1800\,\text{W}\] \[P_{\text{iron}}=1800-800=1000\,\text{W}\]

Initially the machines are sharing load equally. If the field current of first generator is reduced by \(5\%\) and of the second generator increased by \(5\%\), find the sharing of load (MW and MVAR) between the generators. Assume \(X_d = X_q = 0.8\) p.u., no field saturation and rated voltage across load. Reasonable approximations may be made.
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
Rating of each alternator: \[S=100\,\text{MVA}, \qquad \cos\phi=0.8\] Initially, \[P_1=P_2=S\cos\phi =100\times0.8 =80\,\text{MW}\] \[Q_1=Q_2=S\sin\phi =100\times0.6 =60\,\text{MVAR}\] Assuming a base of \(100\,\text{MVA}\), \[V=1\,\text{p.u.}, \qquad I_a=1\,\text{p.u.}\] Since direct-axis and quadrature-axis reactances are equal, the machine is cylindrical rotor with \[X_s=0.8\,\text{p.u.}, \qquad R_a=0\] Initially, \[E_{fA}=E_{fB} = \sqrt{(V\cos\phi+I_aR_a)^2+(V\sin\phi+I_aX_s)^2}\] \[E_{fA}=E_{fB} = \sqrt{(1\times0.8)^2+(1\times0.6+0.8)^2}\] \[E_{fA}=E_{fB}=1.612\,\text{p.u.}\] Assuming linear magnetization characteristics, the change in field current is equal to the change in excitation emf. Generator A excitation is reduced by \(5\%\), \[E'_{fA}=0.95\times1.612 =1.532\,\text{p.u.}\] Generator B excitation is increased by \(5\%\), \[E'_{fB}=1.05\times1.612 =1.693\,\text{p.u.}\] Assuming negligible change in power factor, \[1.532 = \sqrt{(V\cos\phi)^2+(V\sin\phi+I'_aX_s)^2}\] \[I'_a=0.883\,\text{p.u.}\] Hence, the modified active and reactive powers for generator A are \[P'_A=0.883\times40 =35.32\,\text{MW}\] \[Q'_A=0.883\times30 =26.49\,\text{MVAR}\] Similarly, for generator B, \[1.693 = \sqrt{(V\cos\phi)^2+(V\sin\phi+I'_aX_s)^2}\] \[I'_a=1.115\,\text{p.u.}\] Therefore, \[P'_B=1.115\times40 =44.6\,\text{MW}\] \[Q'_B=1.115\times30 =33.45\,\text{MVAR}\] \[\boxed{A:35.32, 26.49, B:44.6, 33.45}\]
Key points
  • Under linear magnetization, percentage change in excitation emf equals percentage change in field current.
  • Active and reactive power sharing are proportional to armature current when the power factor remains approximately constant.

questions.question: In the protection of transformers, harmonic restraint is used to guard against
questions.explanation: When a transformer is energized, a large transient magnetizing current known as inrush current flows. The magnetizing inrush current contains a significant second-harmonic component and may reach several times the rated full-load current. A transformer differential relay responds to current imbalance and may incorrectly interpret the inrush current as an internal fault. To prevent unwanted tripping during transformer energization, harmonic restraint is incorporated in the differential protection scheme. The relay measures the harmonic content of the differential current and blocks operation when the second- harmonic component exceeds a specified threshold. Since harmonic restraint is specifically intended to distinguish magnetizing inrush current from internal faults, it is used to guard against magnetizing inrush current. Hence, the correct option is \[\boxed{\text{(A) magnetizing inrush current}}\]

The input voltage given to a converter is \[v_i = 100\sqrt{2}\sin(100\pi t)\,\text{V}\] The current drawn by the converter is \[\begin{gathered} i_i=10\sqrt{2}\sin\left(100\pi t-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\\ +5\sqrt{2}\sin\left(300\pi t+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\\ +2\sqrt{2}\sin\left(500\pi t-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\,\text{A} \end{gathered}\]

AC-to-DC circulating current dual converters is operated with the following relationship between their triggering angles \((\alpha_1 \text{ and } \alpha_2)\).
questions.explanation:
For a circulating current dual converter, both converters operate simultaneously. To avoid short circuit and to maintain equal average DC output voltages with opposite polarities, \[V_{dc1}+V_{dc2}=0\] For converter 1, \[V_{dc1}=V_{d0}\cos\alpha_1\] For converter 2, \[V_{dc2}=V_{d0}\cos\alpha_2\] Hence, \[V_{d0}\cos\alpha_1+V_{d0}\cos\alpha_2=0\] \[\cos\alpha_1+\cos\alpha_2=0\] \[\cos\alpha_1=-\cos\alpha_2\] \[\alpha_1+\alpha_2=180^\circ\] \[\boxed{\text{A}}\]
Key points
  • In a circulating current dual converter, both converters conduct simultaneously.
  • Average output voltages of the two converters must be equal and opposite.
  • The firing angle relation is \[\alpha_1+\alpha_2=180^\circ.\]

questions.question: The minimum number of wattmeter(s) required to measure \(3\)-phase, \(3\)-wire balanced or unbalanced power is
questions.explanation: For a 3-phase, 3-wire system, the minimum number of wattmeters required to measure total power for both balanced and unbalanced loads is: \[\boxed{2}\] In a 3-phase, 3-wire system: \[I_R+I_Y+I_B=0\] Thus only two line currents are independent, so only two wattmeters are sufficient to measure total power. Using the two-wattmeter method: \[P_{\text{total}}=W_1+W_2\] This method works for: \[\text{Balanced and unbalanced loads}\] and for: \[\text{Leading as well as lagging power factor}\] Therefore, two wattmeters are sufficient for any 3-phase, 3-wire system.

questions.question: If an energy meter disc makes \(10\) revolutions in \(100\) seconds when a load of \(450\,\text{W}\) is connected to it, the meter constant (in rev/kWh) is
questions.explanation: Given, \[P=450\,\text{W},\qquad t=100\,\text{s},\qquad N=10\] Energy consumed: \[E=Pt=450\times100=45000\,\text{J}\] Since, \[1\,\text{kWh}=3.6\times10^6\,\text{J}\] Energy in kWh: \[E=\frac{45000}{3.6\times10^6}=0.0125\,\text{kWh}\] Thus, \[10\ \text{revolutions}\equiv0.0125\,\text{kWh}\] Hence meter constant is \[K=\frac{10}{0.0125}=800\,\text{rev/kWh}\] Therefore, \[\boxed{800\,\text{rev/kWh}}\] Hence, the correct option is \[\boxed{\textbf{D. }800}\]
